title: AI-Assisted Microbiome Analysis with R
text:
Turn prepared microbiome counts into results you can understand and defend. Start with synthetic practice, apply the workflow to a human stool dataset, then adapt it to your own study.






One workflow for every dataset




Define an answerable question and what each sample represents.
Preview the figures and the questions they help answer.
Meet the counts, sample metadata and feature annotations.
Check identifiers, count values, sample quality and study design.
Run exploration, then appropriate statistical analyses.
Verify and explain findings using figures, numbers and limitations.
Write a short report that another researcher can follow.










Example
Your learning goal




Synthetic practice
Understand composition, diversity, community distances and numerical checks


Zackular human stool study
Compare healthy and carcinoma samples; evaluate community and OTU-level associations


Your own study
Define groups, choose covariates and decide whether this workflow fits your design



You begin with prepared integer feature counts, not raw sequences. These pages do not perform read quality control, denoising or taxonomic assignment. Each coloured composition segment represents a feature, not necessarily a named species. All samples remain visible, including unusual observations.
Human → AI → Human: first write your question or interpretation; use AI for a specific explanation or review; then check its response against your files and make the final decision yourself.
Begin: Set up your workspace
crumbs: 1  AI-Assisted Microbiome Analysis with R

title: Set up your workspace
text:
Open the project
Have R, Quarto and VS Code or RStudio installed. Use an R/Bioconductor combination that supplies ANCOMBC 2.16.0 or newer for the expanded inference stage. You may need to update R if your compatible Bioconductor release supplies an older ANCOMBC. Download the project, extract it and open its main folder. Apply this update there before using the new commands. Open a terminal in the folder containing _quarto.yml.
You should see data/, scripts/R/, config/, examples/ and templates/. Run all analysis commands from this folder.

title: Set up your workspace
section: Restore and extend the R environment
text:
Restore and extend the R environment
Start R in the terminal:
R
At the R prompt, restore the existing project lockfile if present, then add the packages needed for this expanded workflow:
options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
if (!requireNamespace("renv", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("renv")
if (file.exists("renv.lock")) renv::restore()
renv::install(c("ggplot2", "vegan"))
renv::install("bioc::ANCOMBC")
renv::snapshot()
renv::status()
Follow installation prompts and resolve errors before continuing. ANCOMBC adds Bioconductor dependencies; installation can take longer than exploration packages. Use a Bioconductor release compatible with your R version. Do not force a development version or replace packages at random to bypass an error.
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggplot2))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(vegan))
packageVersion("ANCOMBC")
stopifnot(packageVersion("ANCOMBC") >= numeric_version("2.16.0"))
q(save = "no")
Commands beginning Rscript or quarto run in the terminal. R expressions such as library() run at the R prompt. Reading a page runs no analysis.

title: Set up your workspace
text:
Keep the work organised
Inputs belong in data/; generated tables and figures in results/; learner writing in ignored reports/. Settings belong in config/. Reruns replace named outputs, so copy an output folder before comparing alternative settings. Do not reuse an incomplete run.
If an error occurs, record the exact command, message, R version and package versions. Ask AI to explain that evidence, then check the proposed remedy.
Next: Synthetic practice

title: Workflow and output map
text:
Three inputs, two analysis stages
feature-counts.tsv has feature_id followed by sample columns of finite, nonnegative integer counts. sample-metadata.tsv has unique sample_id and group, plus covariates. taxonomy.tsv has unique feature_id and taxon. Identifiers connect the files; their row order need not match.
The older numbered scripts can remain for previous examples; the new pages use the entry points above. They share common.R.

title: Workflow and output map
text:
run_workflow.R checks inputs and produces exploration.
run_inference.R checks the completed exploration, unchanged inputs and settings, sample independence and model estimability before testing.

title: Workflow and output map
text:
What changes between analyses?

Composition shows up to 15 features, ranked by mean sample proportion. Other is light grey. Selection is for display, not differential testing.
Shannon and observed richness use all supplied features. Expected richness standardises sampling effort conditional on the supplied table.
PCoA uses Bray–Curtis distances on sample proportions. It uses a Lingoes correction; its axis percentages describe the corrected geometry.
A separate depth sensitivity repeats equal-depth subsampling 20 times and averages Bray–Curtis distances. It does not overwrite original counts.
The heatmap shows log10(proportion + 0.000001), without row scaling. Its offset is for display only. It is not supplied to ANCOM-BC2.
Differential abundance uses unrarefied counts, after a documented prevalence filter, with its own bias correction and sensitivity analysis.

Similar-looking plots can answer different questions. Never use a heatmap’s colours, a PCoA gap or a large composition segment as a significance test.
Warnings are saved in exploration-warnings.txt or inference-warnings.txt when present. Read them before accepting results; model convergence or singularity warnings stop inference. Synthetic rarefaction warnings about the lack of count-one features reflect the supplied teaching table and limit biological interpretation.
tables/feature-model-support.tsv records positive sample counts, positive-subset design rank and effect availability for each fitted OTU. Use it to investigate unestimable effects; a passing whole-study model check does not guarantee every sparse OTU supports every coefficient.

title: Write a report you can defend
text:
Create a draft without overwriting your writing
Run the dataset’s create_report.R command. It creates a draft in ignored reports/ and keeps an existing draft unchanged. The report is independent of the book; you do not add it to _quarto.yml.
Edit the prompts into your own account of the question, inputs, decisions, results, checks, limitations and next scientific action. Keep your report short: use the most informative figures in the narrative and link the rest as supporting evidence.
crumbs: 4  Write a report you can defend

title: Write a report you can defend
text:
Every claim needs a location
For a diversity claim, name the metric, groups, summary and source table. For a community test, record the distance, transformation, model, permutations, R-squared, p-value and dispersion result. For an OTU association, give its ID, tested contrast, natural-log effect, uncertainty, BH-adjusted p-value and pseudo-count sensitivity result. Do not silently substitute a genus name for an OTU-level finding.
Distinguish a descriptive difference from an adjusted association and from a causal claim. Adjustment addresses only the measured variables in that model.
crumbs: 4  Write a report you can defend

title: Write a report you can defend
text:
Render separately
From the project root:
cd reports
quarto render zackular-report.qmd --to html
cd ..
Use synthetic-report.qmd or my-study-report.qmd for the other examples. Check that images load, numerical claims match the current complete run, and all placeholder text has been replaced. New outputs do not update your written interpretations automatically.
crumbs: 4  Write a report you can defend

title: Write a report you can defend
text:
Record AI’s contribution
State the tool/model if known, date, task, what you supplied, what you adopted and how you checked it. First write your own observation; ask AI to challenge it using actual tables; make the final revision yourself. Do not share identifying or restricted participant information.

text:
Stage 1: exploration
From the main project folder:
Confirm exploration-status.txt says COMPLETE. Open all nine figures and match each to its table using the output map. Shannon uses all features; grey Other affects composition display only.
PCoA uses Bray–Curtis on proportions with a Lingoes correction. The depth sensitivity uses 20 equal-depth random subsamples and mean distances. These are different distance definitions, not interchangeable results.

title: 5. Run the analysis: Synthetic practice
text:
Stage 2: inference
Rscript scripts/R/run_inference.R data/synthetic results/synthetic config/synthetic.tsv
The script requires unchanged inputs/settings and a complete exploration. It runs marginal PERMANOVA and dispersion checks for both distance definitions. Read the group term’s R-squared and p-value alongside dispersion and sample structure. These tests do not turn an observational comparison into causation.
Synthetic inference stops after community tests because DA is disabled. Use this to learn how test output relates to distances. Continue to Zackular for the OTU differential-abundance example; do not treat 15 fictional features as validation of ANCOM-BC2.
If any command fails, stop. An incomplete folder can contain files from an earlier run. Preserve the error; do not write conclusions from partial results.
Next: Verify and explain

text:
Explain the exploration
Write one sentence per figure. For composition, compare named OTUs and acknowledge the pooled remainder. For Shannon and richness, check sample values and group summaries. For PCoA, name the distance and axis percentages; check whether the pattern persists in the depth sensitivity. For the heatmap and prevalence plot, distinguish high abundance from frequent detection.

title: 6. Verify and explain: Synthetic practice
text:
Explain the tests
Record the group term’s R-squared and p-value in permanova.tsv, the covariates in model-matrix.tsv, and dispersion results. Compare the two distance definitions without choosing a favourite p-value. Dispersion is not adjusted for the covariates in the PERMANOVA model.
Human → AI → Human task: write your result paragraph first. Give AI the relevant figures, exact table rows, model and contrast. Ask it to identify unsupported numbers, reversed effects and causal wording. Accept changes only after checking them yourself. Finish with one limitation and a useful next scientific question.

Dispersion and differential abundance



Within-group dispersion in both distance definitions.


This checks variability around each group’s spatial median, separately from the adjusted community test. It does not adjust for age, sex or location.

The supplied reference run has no sensitivity-supported discoveries. A point above the adjusted-p threshold is not highlighted unless it also passes the pseudo-count check. Missing model estimates are excluded from the plot.

Locate the three files
Pick one sample and find it in counts and metadata. Pick one feature and find it in counts and taxonomy. Row order is not evidence of a match; IDs are.
Read the study and provenance notes. The input was exported from a packaged count object; the original human study had 90 samples in three groups. Our comparison retains all available healthy and carcinoma samples. Two absent adenoma records do not affect this selection.
Metadata preserve age, sex, collection location and original labels. Sex whitespace was removed and f/m expanded; a location typo was harmonised before modelling. The participant-ID field in the original spreadsheet is empty; do not claim a separately verified participant crosswalk.
Taxonomy identifies OTU annotations, sometimes only at family level. Several OTUs can share a genus name. Do not collapse them by copying legend labels.

title: 5. Run the analysis: Human stool study
text:
Stage 2: inference
Rscript scripts/R/run_inference.R data/zackular results/zackular config/zackular.tsv
The script requires unchanged inputs/settings and a complete exploration. It runs marginal PERMANOVA and dispersion checks for both distance definitions. Read the group term’s R-squared and p-value alongside dispersion and sample structure. These tests do not turn an observational comparison into causation.
ANCOM-BC2 then models unrarefied counts with age + sex + collection_location + group, after 10% prevalence filtering. Positive natural-log group effects mean higher estimated abundance in Carcinoma versus Healthy. BH-adjusted p < 0.05 and pseudo-count sensitivity jointly define highlighted discoveries. Structural-zero calling is disabled; unavailable results are not discoveries.
Open da-volcano.png and da-effects.png only after inference-status.txt says COMPLETE. Up to 20 features appear in the effect plot even if none is significant. These intervals are pointwise, not multiple-testing-adjusted.

title: 6. Verify and explain: Human stool study
section: Read the supplied reference run critically
text:
Read the supplied reference run critically
With 999 permutations and the configured age, sex and location adjustment, the group term explained about 1.99% of corrected distance variation: p = 0.165 for proportions and p = 0.172 for equal-depth sensitivity. The corresponding unadjusted dispersion p-values were 0.420 and 0.428. These results do not establish a group-wide community association at 0.05; they also do not prove that profiles are identical or dispersion equal.
The 10% prevalence filter retained 1,915 OTUs. In the supplied ANCOM-BC2 run, no OTU passed both adjusted-p and conservative pseudo-count sensitivity criteria. Several OTUs have small adjusted p-values but fail the sensitivity check. Do not describe those as robust biomarkers. The package warns during t-distribution p-value calculation. 100 OTUs lack finite group effects or standard errors; their positive-count subsets are rank deficient for the full model. Check feature-model-support.tsv and the raw coefficient table. The learner-facing summary leaves their p-values missing, rather than calling them evidence for no difference. This is a worked review example, not a validated screening test.

title: Appendix A — Methods, decisions and references
text:
Within-sample diversity
For counts \(x_i\), \(p_i=x_i/\sum_j x_j\) and \(H=-\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i)\). Observed richness is the number of positive counts; evenness concerns how abundance is distributed. Shannon is not a health score, and its interpretation depends on the feature definition.
Depth affects detection. Rarefaction curves show expected detected features in smaller samples drawn from the already processed table. They cannot recover discarded features or prove complete biological sampling. The Zackular object has undergone upstream processing; interpret its curves within that limitation. The initial synthetic example has only 15 fictional features, so rapid saturation is a property of the teaching data.
Depth 0 in settings means the smallest supplied sample total. That is a convenience, not a universal recommendation. Inspect low-depth samples first. For Zackular, 15,000 retains every sample. Choose and justify a depth before looking for a favourable group result; record excluded samples if needed.

title: Appendix A — Methods, decisions and references
section: Community composition: PCoA, PERMANOVA and dispersion
text:
Community composition: PCoA, PERMANOVA and dispersion
Bray–Curtis quantifies compositional dissimilarity. PCoA places samples in a low-dimensional representation of that distance. Axes can reverse signs between implementations without changing relationships. No phylogenetic tree is supplied, so this workflow does not calculate UniFrac.
PCoA uses Lingoes-corrected distances. PERMANOVA and dispersion use the same correction. PERMANOVA uses marginal tests (by = "margin"), so the group term is conditional on configured covariates. Its R-squared reports the fraction of total distance variation attributed to the term; it is not classification accuracy. A significant dispersion result can complicate a location-based interpretation. A nonsignificant result does not prove equal dispersion. The separate dispersion test does not adjust for covariates.
Both proportion-based and equal-depth sensitivity results are saved. A change in conclusion is evidence to investigate, not a reason to select the smaller p-value. The sensitivity averages distances across random subsamples; it is not a pooled meta-analysis of repeated tests. Do not compare PCoA axis positions numerically between different distance matrices.
These scripts assume independent observations. Paired samples, repeated visits, shared cages, households and clustered recruitment can require a different model and restricted permutations. Setting design_confirmed to TRUE does not make that assumption correct.

title: Appendix A — Methods, decisions and references
text:
OTU differential abundance
ANCOM-BC2 estimates model-based abundance associations from supplied counts while correcting sampling biases under its assumptions. It does not measure absolute bacterial load. The guide tests OTUs; a genus label is an annotation, not genus-level aggregation.
The Zackular model is age + sex + collection_location + group. Group is internally coded Reference then Comparison. A positive group coefficient means higher estimated abundance in Carcinoma versus Healthy, conditional on those covariates. Effects use natural logarithms, so exp(effect) is a model-estimated fold change; ln(2) is approximately a twofold association. These are not DESeq2’s log2 effects.
Features detected in at least 10% of the 60 samples enter the feature model. BH correction addresses multiple feature tests for each coefficient. A highlighted discovery must have adjusted p < 0.05, the package’s DA indicator and passage through pseudo-count sensitivity (conservative = TRUE). Unavailable effects or standard errors are explicitly flagged with estimate_available = FALSE; their learner-facing p-values are left missing. The package’s original coefficient table is also retained. ANCOMBC may assign p = q = 1 to an unestimable test; that is not evidence for a null effect. Unavailable results are never discoveries. Structural-zero detection is disabled in this example; no manual pseudo-count is added to model inputs. The display offset is unrelated.
Approximate pointwise 95% intervals are effect ± 1.96 standard errors. They are not simultaneous intervals and do not replace adjusted p-values. The forest display ranks up to 20 features by adjusted p-value even when none is a discovery. Do not interpret its ranking as validation of biomarkers.
Only 15 features exist in synthetic practice, and their generating truth is not a validated DA benchmark. Its default inference demonstrates community tests; ANCOM-BC2 is taught with the larger human table. Your own study starts with inference blocked and DA disabled until you justify the design.

title: Appendix A — Methods, decisions and references
text:
Human dataset provenance
Zackular JP et al. (2014), The Human Gut Microbiome as a Screening Tool for Colorectal Cancer. Study. Original study: 90 stools, 30 per clinical group, 16S V4 MiSeq. Original metadata and sequences. The packaged microbiomeutilities::zackular2014 object contains 88 samples and 2,078 OTUs. All sample IDs, disease labels and ages were checked against the original spreadsheet. Two adenoma records are absent, reason unresolved. All 30 healthy and all 30 carcinoma records are retained here.
Its package documentation cites a different 2013 mouse study; use the human citation above. Exact sources and checksums are in data/provenance/zackular/. The spreadsheet’s participant-ID field is empty. Sample-name tokens are unique and consistent with the study design, but are not a validated participant crosswalk. Do not claim a separate participant identity audit.
The exported sex labels were trimmed (including nonbreaking whitespace) and mapped f→Female, m→Male; Ann Arbor,. MI was harmonised to Ann Arbor, MI. Original labels are retained alongside cleaned labels in metadata. These changes were made before modelling, not chosen to improve test results. BMI, medications and other possible confounders are not included in this teaching model. Conclusions remain observational and sample-specific.

title: Appendix A — Methods, decisions and references
text:
What is outside this practical?
Raw-read QC, denoising, contamination assessment, reference-based taxonomy, phylogenetic tree building, functional prediction, microbial networks and predictive-model validation each require additional evidence and workflows.

title: Appendix A — Methods, decisions and references
section: Numerical limitations in the supplied human run
text:
Numerical limitations in the supplied human run
The ANCOMBC t-distribution calculation emitted NaNs produced. The exported summary flags 100 OTUs without finite group estimates or standard errors; all 100 have rank-deficient design matrices when restricted to samples with positive counts. feature-model-support.tsv makes that support visible. Do not interpret the package’s replacement p-values of 1 for unavailable tests as evidence of equality. Other estimable results must still pass the pseudo-count sensitivity criterion. The two-group warning about deactivating multi-group tests is expected: no global or pairwise multi-group analysis was requested. Read both warnings rather than silencing them without explanation.
